cues.text: Raised Between Two Faiths
Born around 903 to Duke Wratislaw, a Christian, and Dragomir, a pagan noblewoman of a neighboring Slavic tribe, Wenceslaus grew up at the very center of Bohemia's unfinished religious transformation.
He grew up in a duchy only recently and unevenly Christianized.
Old pagan loyalties were still very much alive alongside the new faith, and the ruling household itself was split along exactly that same religious line.
Wenceslaus received his own Christian formation chiefly from his devout grandmother, St. Ludmila , who instructed him carefully.
Her instruction shaped the young prince's character so decisively that even the political turmoil surrounding his own accession could not shake the Christian convictions she had planted in him.
A Grandmother's Martyrdom
When Wenceslaus's father died, his pagan mother Dragomir assumed the regency and moved swiftly against the Christian influence Ludmila had exercised over her grandson.
She had the elderly woman murdered in 921.
That killing left the young duke's own family divided by exactly the same religious conflict tearing at his kingdom.
Despite this brutal loss, or perhaps because of it, Wenceslaus's Christian commitment deepened still further.
When Christian nobles moved to force his mother from power and place him fully in charge of the duchy, he took up the government.
He was determined to root Bohemia more firmly still in the faith his grandmother had died defending.
A Gentle and Generous Ruler
As duke, Wenceslaus favored the introduction of German priests and the Latin liturgical rite, and worked to strengthen ties with the wider Christian world.
He became known among his people for a personal generosity toward the poor that later legend would immortalize.

That tradition, celebrated centuries later in the Christmas carol Good King Wenceslas , involved the duke venturing out on a bitter winter's night to bring provisions personally to a poor man on the very feast of St. Stephen.
He is also remembered by tradition as having taken a private vow of chastity, living a life of unusual personal austerity and devotion for a ruling prince of his violent age.
Betrayed by His Own Brother

Wenceslaus's piety and his political alignment with Christian Germany provoked resentment among a faction of pagan Bohemian nobles, who found a willing ally in the duke's own younger brother, Boleslaus , ambitious for the throne himself.
On September 28, 935, at Boleslaus's invitation to a religious feast, Wenceslaus was set upon and struck down by assassins as he made his way to morning prayers at the church door.
He was killed, in the most literal sense, in the very act of going to worship.
A Martyr's Devotion, Born Almost Overnight
The manner of Wenceslaus's death — a devout young ruler cut down by his own brother's treachery on the threshold of a church — struck his contemporaries immediately as martyrdom.
Veneration of him as a saint began almost at once, and reported miracles at his tomb accelerated a devotion that spread rapidly through Bohemia and beyond.
His remains were translated to the Church of St. Vitus in Prague, which grew, under this patronage, into one of the great pilgrimage churches of medieval Central Europe.
Legacy
Wenceslaus was posthumously declared king and became, within a generation of his death, the acknowledged patron saint of Bohemia — a status the modern Czech Republic still honors him with today.
The beloved nineteenth-century carol that bears his name, "Good King Wenceslas," has immortalized him far beyond the borders of his own small duchy.
For millions who have never studied the tangled politics of tenth-century Bohemia, he remains the enduring popular image of a Christian ruler.
His charity toward the poor was real enough to outlast his own violent, all-too-brief reign by more than a thousand years.
Every winter, in schoolyards and churches that have long forgotten his history, his name is still sung as a byword for simple, unglamorous goodness.
